claims.quote: if sowing/planting in the middle of summer, some light shade is preferable during the hottest part of the day, as too much heat can cause lettuces to flower prematurely.

claims.claim: Sow spinach in spring and again in late summer to autumn.
claims.quote: For continuous harvests, sow seeds repeatedly every few weeks in spring and late summer/autumn.

claims.claim: Spinach does best grown in spring or autumn, when short days favour leaves over flowers.
claims.quote: In the Midwest, spinach must be grown in the spring or fall when short days trigger leaf production instead of flowering.
claims.note: Page says 'In the Midwest, spinach must be grown in the spring or fall when short days trigger leaf production'; it is scoped to the Midwest, and the claim drops that.

claims.claim: Check: a houseplant pot that is still wet feels heavier than a dry one.
claims.quote: Drier pots feel lighter than wet ones

claims.claim: Check: learn how heavy the pot is just after watering; wet potting mix is much heavier than dry.
claims.quote: Get familiar with how heavy the pot is right after watering, dry potting mix is much lighter in weight than when it is wet.

claims.claim: Check: potting mix gets noticeably lighter as it dries, so weight shows how wet it still is.
claims.quote: As potting mixtures become dry, a definite loss in weight can be observed.

claims.claim: A houseplant with bad root rot is often not worth saving.
claims.quote: Often the best and most cost effective way of dealing with a plant with root rot is to throw it out.

claims.claim: Fix: before throwing out a failing houseplant, take cuttings from it.
claims.quote: Before you throw away the plant, consider propagating it.

claims.claim: Fix: take houseplant cuttings from healthy stems.
claims.quote: Find some long stems that the plant won’t miss. Go for healthy stems, free of pests and diseases

claims.claim: Check: a dry houseplant pot feels lighter than a wet one.
claims.quote: Drier pots feel lighter than wet ones

claims.claim: Check: dry potting mix is much lighter than wet, so a light pot means dry mix.
claims.quote: Get familiar with how heavy the pot is right after watering, dry potting mix is much lighter in weight than when it is wet.

claims.claim: Check: potting mix loses weight as it dries.
claims.quote: As potting mixtures become dry, a definite loss in weight can be observed.

claims.claim: Check: wilting leaves with brown, crispy edges are signs a houseplant isn’t getting enough water.
claims.quote: Wilted leaves, brown and crispy leaf edges and flowers that fade or fall quickly are all signs that a plant isn’t getting enough water

claims.claim: Check: on a dry houseplant the older leaves at the base often yellow and fall first.
claims.quote: Unlike with overwatering (below), older leaves at the base of a dry plant will often yellow and fall first.

claims.claim: Roots need oxygen, and most plants’ roots die in stagnant (stale, still) water.
claims.quote: All plant roots need oxygen (air) and the root zone in hydroponic cultivation must not only be moist and nutrient-rich but must also be very well aerated. Roots of most plants will die in stagnant water.

claims.claim: Healthy roots on a houseplant cutting (including ones rooted in water) are creamy white and firm.
claims.quote: To check for roots, use a spatula, plant label or small trowel to gently lift your cutting out of its media. Inspect the roots. They should be creamy white and firm.
claims.note: Page covers only Monstera deliciosa cuttings and describes lifting the cutting 'out of its media' (soil, perlite, etc.), not cuttings rooted in water; it doesn't say this for houseplant cuttings in general.

claims.claim: Check: healthy houseplant roots are white; brownish to blackish roots point to root rot.
claims.quote: Off-color (brownish to blackish, or dark yellowish) roots, especially at the root tips, often indicate that root rot is present. Healthy roots should be white, entirely so or at least under their outer covering.

claims.claim: Check: rotting roots are soft and brown and may smell bad.
claims.quote: Careful examination of the root systems of these plants reveals roots that are soft and brown. These roots may have a bad odor.

claims.claim: Check/fix: for a houseplant growing in plain water, change the water when it turns cloudy.
claims.quote: Pros: In water, you can observe root growth, the plants are also easy to care for and they don’t require much space. The water should be changed when it becomes cloudy.
claims.note: Page covers only Monstera deliciosa cuttings rooted in water ('monstera cuttings can be rooted in plain water'), not houseplants grown long-term in water.

claims.claim: Fix: for a houseplant grown in water (lucky bamboo), change the water every week.
claims.quote: Change the water weekly.

claims.claim: Fix: a water-rooted houseplant with root rot may not survive, so take a new cutting.
claims.quote: A cutting with root rot may not survive and you may have to take a new cutting.
claims.note: Page covers only Monstera deliciosa cuttings, and links root rot to overwatering or a container that 'is not draining well' (rooting media); it doesn't refer to water-rooted plants.

claims.claim: Fix: take the new cutting from healthy material.
claims.quote: When propagating any plant, choose healthy material.

claims.claim: Fix: for a houseplant in plain water, keep it topped up so the lower stem stays under water.
claims.quote: Keep water topped so that lower part of cutting is always below water surface.
claims.note: Page is about rooting stem cuttings in water before potting them up ('When cuttings have a small network of roots, plant each in a three inch container'), not about houseplants kept in plain water long-term.

claims.claim: Fix: a houseplant grown in plain water (lucky bamboo) should have its roots covered by water.
claims.quote: The stems of lucky bamboo should be submerged in enough water to cover the roots and at least one inch of the stem.
